md: A pregnancy needs six things to happen in order, from an ovum maturing to the embryo implanting. Every method of contraception breaks one link, and naming the link is the mechanism mark.

The **pill** and the **implant** supply **hormones** that stop an ovum maturing and being released. A **condom** is a barrier: no sperm reach the vagina. A **vasectomy** (male sterilisation) cuts the **sperm tubes**, so the semen carries no sperm. **Female sterilisation** cuts the **oviducts**, so the ovum and the sperm cannot meet.

stem: Explain how a contraceptive implant prevents pregnancy. [2]

steps.working: It releases hormones into the woman's blood.
steps.decision: The cause first: an implant is a chemical method, like the pill.

steps.working: The hormones stop ovulation, so no ovum is released to be fertilised.
steps.decision: Then the consequence, the link it breaks: a cause on its own is half an answer.

prompt: A man uses a condom. Which link in the chain does it break?
options: sperm being deposited in the vagina
answer: sperm being deposited in the vagina
explain: Find the link the method acts on, as the worked answer did: a condom is a barrier, so the sperm never reach the vagina. No sperm there, no fertilisation.

optionNotes.why: It tempts because the implant works at that link, but a condom acts on the man, not on the woman's ovaries.
It tempts because it is the last link, but a condom stops the sperm long before there is any embryo.

sperm being made in the testes
twin.answer: sperm being deposited in the vagina
twin.explain: The sperm tubes are cut, so the semen that reaches the vagina carries no sperm. The testes still make sperm, and the woman's ovaries are untouched.

optionNotes.why: It tempts because no sperm come out, but the testes still make sperm; the cut tubes stop them leaving.
It tempts because that link can be broken too, but a vasectomy is an operation on the man.

caption: CCEA's three groups, with one drawback each. Other boards sort by hormonal and non-hormonal: use CCEA's words.

md: CCEA sorts methods by how they work. A barrier is **mechanical**: the male and female condom. A method working through hormones is **chemical**: the pill and the implant. An operation is **surgical**: a vasectomy and female sterilisation. Each has a cost in use, and an answer weighing one up gives the reason with it.

stem: Compared with the male condom, what is one advantage of the contraceptive implant, and one disadvantage? [2]

steps.working: Advantage: it works for years with nothing to remember or put on, so in real use it rarely fails.
steps.decision: An advantage with its reason: the reason shows why it matters.

steps.working: Disadvantage: it has to be fitted under the skin by a nurse or doctor, so she cannot simply start or stop it herself.
steps.decision: A drawback of the implant itself, again with its reason.

title: GCSE Biology Revision "Contraception"
why: A second pass over the methods. It is made for another board: it sorts them as hormonal and non-hormonal and names methods CCEA does not use, so translate each back into the three groups here.

prompt: A condom and a vasectomy both work without hormones. Which of CCEA's groups are they in?
explain: CCEA sorts by how a method works, not by hormones, as the grid shows: a barrier is mechanical and an operation is surgical. So the condom is mechanical and the vasectomy surgical.

optionNotes.why: It tempts because neither uses hormones, but a vasectomy is an operation, and CCEA calls operations surgical.
It tempts because a vasectomy is surgical, but a condom is a barrier, which CCEA calls mechanical.

twin.prompt: The pill and the implant both release hormones. Which of CCEA's groups are they in?
twin.explain: A method that works through hormones is chemical in CCEA's grouping, whether it is swallowed or placed under the skin.

optionNotes.why: It tempts because an implant is a small object in the body, but it works through the hormones it releases, so it is chemical.
It tempts because an implant is put in by a professional, but nothing is cut: it works through hormones.

title: Why only a barrier stops infections
md: An infection passes between two people in body fluids. A condom stops anything passing between them, so it is the only method here that also protects against **sexually transmitted infections**. The pill, the implant and sterilisation act inside one body, and give no protection.
Know which cause is which: **bacteria** cause chlamydia, gonorrhoea and syphilis; **viruses** cause HIV (which leads to AIDS), HPV and herpes. Untreated chlamydia can itself cause infertility.

stem:
(a) Explain why a vasectomy gives no protection against sexually transmitted infections. [1]
(b) Explain how a condom helps to stop the spread of HIV. [1]

steps.working: (a) It puts no barrier between the two people, so infected body fluids can still pass between them.
steps.decision: Cutting the sperm tubes changes nothing about contact: only a barrier stops an infection passing.

steps.working: (b) It is a barrier, so body fluids carrying the virus cannot pass from one partner to the other.
steps.decision: The same idea the other way round: the barrier is what protects.

prompt: Which method protects against HIV as well as against pregnancy?
explain: Only a barrier stops an infection passing between partners, as the worked answer said, and the condom is the only barrier among the three.

optionNotes.why: It tempts because it is very reliable against pregnancy, but it works through hormones inside one body and stops no infection.
It tempts because it is permanent and reliable, but it puts no barrier between the partners.

twin.prompt: Which of these infections is caused by a virus?
twin.explain: Herpes is caused by a virus, like HIV and HPV. Gonorrhoea and chlamydia are caused by bacteria.

optionNotes.why: It tempts because it is sexually transmitted too, but gonorrhoea is caused by a bacterium.
It tempts because it is the infection named most often, but chlamydia is caused by a bacterium.

text: Higher: when a couple cannot conceive

md: Infertility has causes on both sides. In a woman: no ova released, **blocked oviducts**, a **hostile vagina** in which sperm do not survive, or too little of the hormones. In a man: too few sperm, sperm without **flagella** that cannot swim, or **erectile dysfunction**. Untreated infections can cause it in either.

stem:
Higher. (a) A woman's oviducts are blocked. Suggest why in vitro fertilisation can help her to have a baby. [1]
(b) Suggest one other reason a couple might use in vitro fertilisation. [1]

steps.working: (a) Sperm cannot reach her ova in the oviduct; in vitro fertilisation joins them outside her body, so the blockage does not matter.
steps.decision: Say what the blockage stops, then why the treatment gets round it.

steps.working: (b) She does not release ova without help: the treatment's hormones make several mature.
steps.decision: Any cause the treatment can get round earns it.

prompt: A man's sperm have no flagella. Why can he not father a child naturally?
options: the sperm cannot swim to the ovum
answer: the sperm cannot swim to the ovum
explain: Like the worked answer, say what the fault stops. The flagellum is the tail that drives a sperm, so without it no sperm swims up the oviduct to the ovum.

optionNotes.why: It tempts because he is infertile, but his testes still make sperm; they just cannot swim.
It tempts because something is missing from the sperm, but the flagellum is the tail, and the nucleus with its chromosomes is still there.

twin.prompt: A woman's vagina is hostile to sperm. Why can she not become pregnant naturally?
options: the sperm die before they reach the ovum
twin.answer: the sperm die before they reach the ovum
twin.explain: A hostile vagina kills sperm or stops them moving, so none survive the journey to the ovum.

optionNotes.why: It tempts because it is another cause of infertility, but a hostile vagina acts on the sperm, not on the ovaries.
It tempts because it also stops a pregnancy, but the problem comes first: the sperm die before fertilisation.

md: The woman is given **hormones** so that **several ova** mature, and the ova are collected from her ovaries. **Sperm are added in a Petri dish** of nutrient fluid, where fertilisation happens. Each embryo is **left a few days** to divide into a ball of cells and **checked** for normal development; then **several embryos** are placed in the **uterus**.

prompt: Which step of in vitro fertilisation is this, and where is it happening?

stem: Higher. Describe what happens in in vitro fertilisation between collecting the ova and placing embryos in the woman's uterus. [4]

steps.working: Sperm are added to the ova in a Petri dish.
steps.decision: Name the container: 'in a laboratory' has earned nothing.

steps.working: A sperm nucleus joins an ovum nucleus: fertilisation.
steps.decision: Say that fertilisation happens, there in the dish.

steps.working: Each embryo is left for a few days to divide into a ball of cells.
steps.decision: The division takes days, and the wait is a marking point.

steps.working: The embryos are checked to see they are developing normally.
steps.decision: Only embryos developing normally are chosen to go back.

prompt: Why are several embryos placed in the uterus, not just one?
options: to raise the chance that one implants
because one embryo is too small to survive
answer: to raise the chance that one implants
explain: Not every embryo implants, so placing several raises the chance that one will, the same reason several ova are collected at the start. The risk is a multiple birth.

optionNotes.why: It tempts because twins can happen, but they are a risk of the treatment, not its aim.

optionNotes.option: because one embryo is too small to survive
optionNotes.why: It tempts because an early embryo is tiny, but size is not the problem: many embryos simply fail to implant.

twin.prompt: Why does the Petri dish hold a nutrient fluid?
options: to keep the sperm, ova and early embryos alive
to make the sperm swim faster
twin.answer: to keep the sperm, ova and early embryos alive
twin.explain: Everything in the dish is alive and needs feeding until the embryos go back into the uterus, several days later.

optionNotes.option: to make the sperm swim faster
optionNotes.why: It tempts because sperm need energy to swim, but the fluid's job is to keep every cell in the dish alive.
It tempts because fertilisation happens in the fluid, but it is the sperm that fertilise the ova.

md: A method has two failure rates: how often it fails when used perfectly, and how often in real life. The gap is people: a pill forgotten, a condom put on late. An implant or a sterilisation leaves nothing to forget, so its two rates are close.

Some people will not use contraception or fertility treatment for **religious or moral** reasons. When a question asks for an **ethical** reason, cost and side effects are not ethical: in Summer 2025 some answers never gave one.

stem:
Use the table. (a) Which method is the most reliable in real use? [1]
(b) Suggest one reason why the contraceptive pill's real-use rate is higher than its expected rate. [1]

steps.working: (a) The implant: 0.1 pregnancies per 100 women a year, the lowest in real use.
steps.decision: Read the real-use column, not the expected one.

steps.working: (b) Some women forget to take a pill, or take it late.
steps.decision: The gap between the columns is people; a stomach upset that stops the pill working also counts.

prompt: In the table, why does female sterilisation fail about as rarely in real use as expected?
options: there is nothing for the woman to remember or do
answer: there is nothing for the woman to remember or do
explain: The gap between the columns is people, as the worked answer read it. Once the oviducts are cut there is nothing to forget or get wrong, so real use matches expected use.

optionNotes.why: It tempts because it is so reliable, but sterilisation puts no barrier between partners, so it blocks no infection.
It tempts because the chemical methods are reliable too, but sterilisation is surgical: the oviducts are cut.

twin.prompt: In the table, why is the male condom's real-use rate so much higher than its expected rate?
options: it can be put on wrongly or too late
twin.answer: it can be put on wrongly or too late
twin.explain: Used perfectly a condom rarely fails; used by real people it can be put on late, torn or slip, so the real-use rate is far higher.

optionNotes.why: It tempts because the pill's rates also differ, but a condom is a barrier with no hormones in it.
